EAW BRANCH SUPPLEMENT

AN APPRECIATION
from MISS MARY GEORGE

AS this is the last occasion when I shall be contributing to The Electrical Age as EAW Director I do want to say how much I have valued the contact I have had with readers through my regular articles. All big organisations need a journal or bulletin as a means of disseminating news and information to all those concerned with their activities.

brief_context: Mentioned as the editor of the journal since 1956.
brief_extract: All big organisations need a journal or bulletin as a means of disseminating news and information to all those concerned with their activities. The Electrical Age has filled this purpose faithfully and efficiently ever since its inception in 1926 and I would like to pay my own special tribute to Phyllis Thompson who has been its editor since 1956. One of the important tasks of The Electrical Age is to provide an essential link between EAW members and branches through the Branch Supplement, which records news of branch doings and area events and encourages individual contributions from members who perhaps have never seen themselves in print before.

brief_extract: In an interview with the Editor of The Electrical Age Mrs McMullan spoke of her very varied experiences and of her hopes of the contribution which the EAW can make to the community. It is a happy coincidence for the EAW that you were born in Newcastle-upon-Tyne and that you had your early education there since the EAW was launched in the London home of Sir Charles Parsons, famous for his work with the steam turbine, and we have two branches in Newcastle. Indeed, the Afternoon Branch was one of the earliest of our branches having been founded in 1927.

brief_extract: I also publicised the Centenary celebrations of the Cremation Society of Great Britain in 1974, which were attended by delegates from fifteen foreign and Commonwealth countries. Not surprisingly, Osbert Lancaster found the idea of ‘celebrating’ the centenary of cremation worthy of a superb cartoon which appeared on the front page of the Daily Express on the opening day of the conference! A Family Story from 1825

by IAN RITCHIE

FIFTY years ago, when other communities in and around the Vale of Avalon had their main thoroughfares lit by gaslight, Street — a Somerset village in which two Quaker brothers, Cyrus and James Clark, had established a shoe-making business a hundred years before that — was brilliantly lit by electricity. This was entirely due to the fact that the Clark family, who have been pioneers in numerous technical and educational innovations, bought the first dynamo for generating power at their factory in 1911.

brief_context: Author of the book 'C & J Clark 1825-1975'.
article_title: The Life and Work of Alice Clark
brief_extract:
This remarkable and kindly lady took an active part in the everyday running of the business and also took a personal interest in the well-being of the young people of Street. In his book ‘C & J Clark 1825-1975’ Brendan Lehane writes:
‘Alice Clark, who worked in various departments of the firm after joining it in 1893 at the age of 19 and who had campaigned keenly for women’s suffrage, took special interest in the personnel side, and was closely involved with the opening, in 1914 (years before such courses became compulsory), of the Day Continuation School, to whose running costs the firm contributed more than half. ‘Here, from the ages of 14 to 16, boys and girls in the factory came for a day a week (later increased to half their time).

article_title: The Life and Work of Alice Clark
brief_extract:
An earnest wish to improve the quality of their employees’ lives was repaid, in the next generation, by a work-force as well educated as any in the country.’
Alice Clark died in 1934, in her sixtieth year. She left her property to her sister, Dr Hilda Clark, expressing a wish and a suggestion that a swimming pool might be established in Street, with special reference to its usefulness to girls and women. Dr Hilda Clark saw that the suggestion was carried out and Greenbank Pool was opened in April 1937.

brief_context: Mentioned in relation to the British Blacklist.
article_title: The Life and Work of Alice Clark
brief_extract:
It has been written of her:
‘Throughout a very active life she took a delight in what was beautiful and in any good thing that was going — games, country pursuits, the garden, expeditions. Children loved her.’
Incidentally, her sister, Dr Hilda Clark, had the doubtful distinction of having her name on Hitler’s British Blacklist, discovered after the second world war. Why her name was among the list of those considered to be enemies of Nazism and so due for destruction is difficult to imagine, unless her work for refugees after the first war — with sister Alice — marked her as potentially hostile in the event of the occupation of our shores.

brief_context: The unit of force is named after him.
brief_extract:
A water wheel in the path of a stream extracts some of the kinetic energy from the water and starts to turn to grind corn or generate electricity by turning the magnet in a dynamo. Measuring Energy
Energy comes in several forms including mechanical energy, heat, light, sound and electricity and the unit to measure them is the Joule, the work a force of one Newton does in moving through one metre. An oil tanker may carry about 1,000 gallons of oil or about 160 thousand million Joules of energy, and since a Giga-Joule equals one thousand million Joules, an oil tanker carries 160 Giga-Joules.

brief_context: Escorted the group to the Children's Carnival.
brief_extract: Not having any magisterial duties in the island I found it immensely amusing. Sister escorted us to the Children's Carnival and was even more excited than we were. Among my own 'treasures' is a brilliant feather of the Scarlet Ibis, a bird peculiar to the island, which I was lucky enough to pick up out of the swamp, a seed pod 18" long which children use as maracas, a brooch fashioned from the top of a coconut given as a President's farewell, a wood rose from Arima branch, stones and a shell from the beach, a small piece of coral from a reef off Tobago where we bathed and watched exotic fish through a glass bottomed boat, a recipe book of Caribbean dishes and a swizzle stick with a rum punch recipe on the top.

THE coming of June is generally a sign that summer has at last begun in earnest. Except for residents in Scotland and Northern England, we have seen the last of frosts for a few months so that it is safe to plant out all the half hardy annuals.

brief_context: Author of a recent article regarding the Savill Garden.
brief_extract: Its immense interest to all garden lovers deserves an elaboration on that terse description. Lanning Roper in a recent article in ‘The Garden’ says that Sir Eric Savill saw in 1931 the enormous potential of virgin soil, remarkable undulating terrain, fine forest trees, predominantly oak, beech and Scots Pine and water which could be controlled to form lakes and streams. With this backdrop a unique opportunity presented itself to the garden’s creator and he made the most of it.

brief_context: The late creator of the Inverewe garden in Wester Ross.

My two favourite Scottish gardens are Crathes Castle 14 miles (22 km) west of Aberdeen just north of the A93 on the north bank of the River Dee, and Inverewe in Wester Ross, which was created by the late Osgood Mackenzie; it is noted for the sub-tropical plants. Inverewe is 7 miles (11 km) from Gairloch and 36 miles (52 km) from Achnasheen Station and is well worth making a detour of many miles to see.

brief_context: A local resident whose home was early to have electricity.
article_title: VISIT TO SEEBOARD MILNE MUSEUM, TONBRIDGE
brief_extract: Along the West wall is a mural which, in abstract form, depicts the development of electricity from natural elements, the harnessing of lighting, generation, distribution and utilisation, through to the production of atomic energy and to future sources of supply. Of particular interest to members was a piece of information gleaned about David Saloman, a local resident whose home was the second one in the country to be lit by electricity. Members also learned that in 1895 he officially opened the local electricity power house, driving there in a motor car at 5 mph preceded by a man carrying a red flag.

brief_extract:
The Way Ahead

— from the first National Energy Conference

by ANN McMULLAN
Director EAW

Buckinghamshire Advertiser

THE EAW, as one of four women's organisations invited to participate in the first National Energy Conference convened last June by Mr. Anthony Wedgwood Benn, the Secretary of State for Energy, was pleased at its inclusion in a necessarily limited invitation list, and honoured by this Government recognition of its role in helping to create informed public opinion concerning the domestic uses of electricity in the community.

title: Sir
brief_context: Speaker who queried the practice of forecasting.
brief_extract: Despite the unemotional tone of the debate one could easily detect the differences in the philosophies of the energy industries, as well as many other cross-currents of feeling between Government, industries and consumers. First in to bat was Sir Arthur Hetherington, at that time Chairman of the British Gas Corporation, who queried the whole practice of forecasting, regarding as especially suspect any forecast of "a constant relationship between supply and demand". Sir Arthur was followed by Sir Arthur Hawkins, Chairman of the Central Electricity Generating Board, who declared that there was no stronger supporter for an energy policy than the CEGB.

brief_extract: First in to bat was Sir Arthur Hetherington, at that time Chairman of the British Gas Corporation, who queried the whole practice of forecasting, regarding as especially suspect any forecast of "a constant relationship between supply and demand". Sir Arthur was followed by Sir Arthur Hawkins, Chairman of the Central Electricity Generating Board, who declared that there was no stronger supporter for an energy policy than the CEGB. All, he said, were agreed that the national interest was paramount and he went on to remind the Conference that electricity (unlike coal, gas or oil) is used by virtually everyone.

brief_context: Author of the article about the New Zealand dairy industry.
brief_extract:
The Clipper Dunedin which brought the first refrigerated cargo from New Zealand to Britain in 1882. 12,000 Miles and 150 Years
by SUSAN EXCELL

The story of the New Zealand dairy industry from the early 19th century. MOST of you will have seen New Zealand butter and cheese in the shops with the familiar red and green "Anchor" emblem on the wrapper, but have you ever wondered how a country more than 12,000 miles away from Britain can send such large amounts of dairy produce to the United Kingdom and still sell it in perfect condition and at competitive prices?

title: Reverend
brief_context: Established a mission north of Auckland in 1814.
brief_extract:
This particular venture was very successful and began the real development of New Zealand's dairy industry—leading to the time when New Zealand became not only Britain's biggest supplier of butter and cheese but also the world's largest supplier of dairy produce. It Started in 1814
However, the true origins of the New Zealand dairy industry go back long before 1882, in fact to 1814, when a certain Reverend Samuel Marsden from Britain arrived in New Zealand to establish a mission north of Auckland. He brought with him two cows and a bull — the first dairy cattle to settle in New Zealand.

title: Mr
brief_context: Bought a Jersey calf called Jenny in 1876.
brief_extract: He brought with him two cows and a bull — the first dairy cattle to settle in New Zealand. After organised colonisation began in 1840 more cattle were imported and although the first Jersey cattle set foot in New Zealand in 1862, it was not till 1876 that real interest was shown in this particular breed when a Mr Hulke bought a young Jersey calf called Jenny in a sale, put a halter on her and walked her on foot to his home 130 miles away in Taranaki. He could not possibly have foreseen what a buy he had made as he trudged all those miles.

brief_context: Pioneer Jersey breeder who established the breed in Taranaki.

EAW BRANCH SUPPLEMENT

DIRECTION FINDING

ALL of us at some time or other are asked
to give someone directions in finding
their way. Sometimes the goal may be just
around the corner, sometimes it is some miles
away.

brief_context: Author of a featured article in this issue
brief_extract:
A great many signposts have been set
up in consumer country but very often they seem
to be pointing in different directions. All consumers will find the EAW Director's
article in this issue of special value since it
analyses the consumer scene and the role of the
EAW in putting consumers on the right road. The current campaign theme 'EAW in the
Community' indicates that the Association is
concerned with all sections of society and has
something practical to offer to meet particular
needs.

brief_context: Author, Director of EAW and depicted as a glider pilot.
brief_extract:
EAW AND THE CONSUMER SCENE

by ANN McMULLAN, Director EAW

Taking off as a pupil glider pilot

'When I use a word' Humpty Dumpty said
in rather scornful tone, 'it means just what I
choose it to mean - neither more nor less.'
'The question is,' said Alice, 'whether you
can make words mean so many different
things.' ('Through the Looking Glass': Lewis Carroll)

CONSUMERISM is one of today's
words which might well cause Alice
to pose that question. The EAW was one of the earliest consumer
voices in this country and through its ideas,
education programmes, branch activities,
opinions and sometimes its criticisms, the
Association has made a significant contribution
to the development of home electricity as we
know it today.

Standards and Exports
In a foreword to the BSI Annual Report the President, Baroness Seear, stressed the vital contribution which standards can make to Britain's export based economic recovery.
